title: Enhancing Interpretability and Generalizability in Extended Isolation Forests
summary: The paper addresses the lack of interpretability and generalization in Extended Isolation Forest anomaly detection. It proposes ExIFFI, a DIFFI-style feature-importance method for any hyperplane-splitting isolation forest, and EIF+, which samples EIF split intercepts from N(E[A], ησ(A)) instead of a uniform interval. Across 16 benchmarks, EIF+ improves Average Precision over EIF when trained only on inliers, e.g., Bisect reaches 1.00 vs 0.99 in Scenario II.

match_target.why: C1 is the cheapest direct test of the paper's central generalization claim: Bisect Scenario II has only 1,100 points and 6 features, so one EIF+ fit is CPU-fast; C2 supplies the EIF baseline (0.99), making the target 1.00 vs 0.99 improvement visible.

tolerance.why: Rule 3: Average Precision is a bounded score on the 1,100-example Bisect dataset, and the paper prints it as a fraction in [0,1]; use ±0.02 absolute.

requirements.stmt: For EIF+, at each node draw α from N(E[A], ησ(A)), where A={x·v}, and set p=αv; do not use the uniform min/max interval.
requirements.quote: EIF+draws it from a normal distribution N(E[A], ησ(A)) as shown in Figure 1b.

requirements.stmt: For the EIF baseline, draw α uniformly between min and max of the projections {x·v} and set p=αv.
requirements.quote: α ∈[min {x · v ∀x ∈X}, max {x · v ∀x ∈X}], p = αv.

requirements.stmt: At each node draw a unit normal vector v by normalizing a d-dimensional standard Gaussian vector.
requirements.quote: As done in [39, 19], we first select a random hyperplane by drawing a unit vector v defined as in (6). which will serve as the normal vector of the hyperplane.

requirements.stmt: Split a node by L={x | v·x > v·p} and R=X\L; recurse until stopping.
requirements.quote: Thus the hyperplane splits the dataset Xt into two subsets,

requirements.stmt: Compute anomaly score as s(x,ñ)=2^{-E(h(x))/c(ñ)} with c(N)=2H(N−1)−2(N−1)/N and H(i)=ln(i)+0.5772156649.
requirements.quote: Then, as IF does [38], the EIF algorithm uses the average depth of the point in each tree to evaluate the anomaly score

requirements.stmt: Fit only on the inlier subset and evaluate Average Precision on the full labeled dataset (no holdout).
requirements.quote: We fit the models exclusively on the inliers within the dataset, that correspond to the scenario of 0 contamination of outliers.

requirements.stmt: Use Average Precision over all samples, not accuracy or thresholded F1.
requirements.quote: Subsequently, we assess the Average Precision scores of these models when applied to the entirety of the dataset.

requirements.stmt: Allow EIF+ to create empty branches; do not prune or resample to avoid them.
requirements.quote: Even if EIF+can generate empty branches, they contribute to the formation of a model that exhibits enhanced generalizability

requirements.stmt: For ExIFFI, assign node importance λ_k(x)=(|X_k|/|L_k|)abs(v_k) if v_k·x>v_k·p_k, else (|X_k|/|R_k|)abs(v_k); sum over path and trees.
requirements.quote: Thus, we assign an importance value function to every node of the trees that is the projection on the normal vector of the splitting hyperplane of the quotient between the cardinality of the sample before a particular node and after it, following the path of a sample x.

requirements.stmt: Normalize cumulative importance vectors by the sum of orthogonal vectors V(x); compute GFI=Î_O/Î_I.
requirements.quote: the vectors of importance have to be divided by the sum of the orthogonal vectors.

requirements.stmt: Compute AUCFS as AUCM−AUCL by iteratively removing most/least important features and evaluating Average Precision.
requirements.quote: AUCFS is calculated as the difference between the area under the curve when shrinking the dimensions of the dataset on the most important features
